note: Part B (drawing) is not transcribed: no model answer exists.

questions.text: The figure shows illustrations of six metal rods which have internal or external screw thread patterns at their ends. The shaded portion in the figure shows the cross section view. What is the maximum length possible by connecting the rods? Threads cannot be connected partially.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The two 220 rods have internal (female) threads at both ends, so each can only sit where two male ends point into it, and a chain can hold at most one of them. The four 200 rods have a male thread on top (outside the 200 dimension, so it adds no length once screwed in) and a female thread at the bottom. Matching thread type (coarse or fine, and the slant of the thread lines) gives the chain: rod 3 into rod 4 into the second 220 rod, and rod 5 into rod 6 into the other end of the same 220 rod. All four 200 rods and one 220 rod are used: 4 x 200 + 220 = 1020.

questions.text: The attached image shows a corridor floor that is covered with square tiles of the same size. How many tiles are covered by the green patch?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: The corridor is 6 tiles wide (one orange border tile on each side and 4 white tiles). The green patch spans 6 rows of tiles, which get shorter with distance. Top row: 5 tiles (the right border tile is not green). The next 4 rows: all 6 tiles each, 24 tiles. Bottom row: 4 tiles (the left border tile and the white tile next to it are uncovered). Total 5 + 24 + 4 = 33.

questions.text: Figure to the left shows an unfolded pattern of a die. If four such identical dice are stacked one on top of another, as shown on the right, what is the sum of the numbers appearing on the faces which are parallel to the ground?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: From the net, opposite faces are 1 and 5, 4 and 3, 6 and 2. For each die the two horizontal faces are the pair whose numbers are not seen on the two visible side faces. Top die (sides 4 and 2): top and bottom are 5 and 1, sum 6. Second die (sides 4 and 5): 6 and 2, sum 8. Third die (sides 3 and 6): 1 and 5, sum 6. Bottom die (sides 1 and 2): 4 and 3, sum 7. Total 6 + 8 + 6 + 7 = 27.

questions.text: Twenty points are arranged on a plane as shown in the figure below. What is the highest number of squares that can be drawn using any four points as corners?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: The points form a plus shape on a 6 by 6 grid (a 2 by 6 band across and a 6 by 2 band down the middle). Squares with sides along the grid: only the 9 unit squares fit, since any bigger one needs a point outside the plus. Tilted squares: 4 with side \(\sqrt{2}\), 2 with side \(\sqrt{5}\), 4 with side \(\sqrt{8}\) and 2 with side \(\sqrt{13}\). Total 9 + 4 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 21.

questions.text:
Area of black surface in the following image is ________ cm².
Note:
1. All curves have same radii.
2. Use the value of pi as 22/7
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The figure is made of four 7 cm squares in a pinwheel. In each square the triangle on one side of the diagonal is black (24.5 cm²). The curves are arcs of radius 7 cm centred on a square corner. A curved sliver cut from the white half stays black inside the square, and an identical sliver is attached outside the square; each sliver is a 45° right triangle of area 24.5 minus a 45° sector of area \(\frac{1}{8} \cdot \frac{22}{7} \cdot 49 = 19.25\), so 5.25 cm². Each square therefore gives 24.5 + 5.25 + 5.25 = 35 cm², and four squares give 140 cm².

questions.text: The image is a ceramic tile of dimension 20 cm x 20 cm. How many distinct patterns can you create by using two such ceramic tiles in a rectangular patch of 40 cm x 20 cm on the wall?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The tile is split along a diagonal into a black half and a grey half, so it can be laid in 4 orientations, one for each corner the black half can sit in. The two tiles side by side in the 40 cm x 20 cm patch can each take any of the 4 orientations independently, so the number of patterns is 4 x 4 = 16. Each pattern is counted as it sits on the wall, so a pattern and its half-turn are counted as two different patterns.

questions.text: A cube is created by stacking 27 smaller cubes as shown in the figure. A plane, going through vertices A, B and C, cuts the cube as shown in the figure. How many smaller cubes will get cut?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: A is the top front-left corner, B the top back-right corner and C the bottom front-right corner, so the plane cuts off the corner where these three meet. Using coordinates 0 to 3, the plane is \(x - y + z = 3\). A small cube is cut when the plane passes through its inside, which happens for 6 cubes in one layer of the diagonal and 3 in the next. Total 9 cubes.

questions.text: At most how many triangles can appear by adding two straight lines to the figure?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: The M shape has four strokes. One line crossing all four strokes makes 3 triangles (one at each peak and one at the valley). A second line, placed to cross all four strokes and the first line, creates triangles with every pair of non-parallel strokes and with the first line as well. Trying the best positions, the most that can be reached is 10 triangles.

questions.text: How many distinct motifs appear in the figure on the right? Flips and rotations are to be counted separately, for example the motifs P and Q are distinct.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: All 18 motifs share the same central core; they differ in the petals on the left and right sides (whether a side has a petal coming out of the upper joint, a horizontal petal, a petal turning up or down from its tip, or a petal coming out of the lower joint). Grouping motifs with identical side petals gives groups of sizes 4, 4, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1 and 1 (18 motifs). So 8 distinct motifs appear.

questions.text: A family of four—grandfather, father, son and daughter—are caught in a heavy rain and are stranded at a bus stop close to their home. However they have only one umbrella with them. The umbrella can take a maximum of two people without either of them getting wet. The four members of the family take different times to walk from bus stop to home. The grandfather is slowest of all, taking 10 minutes, followed by the father who takes 5 minutes. The son takes 2 minutes, while the daughter takes only a minute. What is the minimum total time (in minutes) for all four members of the family to reach home without any of them getting wet?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: A pair walks at the speed of the slower one, and someone must bring the umbrella back. Best plan: daughter and son go (2), daughter returns (1), grandfather and father go together (10), son returns (2), daughter and son go (2). Total 2 + 1 + 10 + 2 + 2 = 17 minutes.

questions.text: Six cards are laid out on a table as shown in the figure below. Each of the cards has a number on one side and a letter on the other side. What is the minimum number of cards you need to flip and see to make sure the rule, “cards that have a vowel on one side always have an even number on the other side” is TRUE?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The cards show 3, M, 7, E, 8, R. The rule fails only if a vowel sits behind an odd number. So E must be checked (its back must be even), and the odd numbers 3 and 7 must be checked (their backs must not be vowels). M and R can have anything behind them, and 8 is even, so a vowel behind it breaks nothing. Three cards.

questions.text: X1 is a 3D form generated from the shape X, using certain 3D operations. It has 14 surfaces in total. If the same operations are carried out on shape Y, how many surfaces would the resulting 3D form have?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: In X1 each diagonal pair of squares is swept up and over into an arch, and the two arches cross. The top faces of the two arches merge into one surface and so do the inner faces, while each arch's two side faces are cut into two by the other arch: 1 + 1 + 8 + 4 end faces = 14. In Y the squares sit at 45° to the arch, giving a bar with a ridge on top, and the quarter circles give a bar with two flat faces and one curved face. No faces are level with each other, so nothing merges: the square bar's two upper faces are split (4) and its lower two are not (2); the quarter-circle bar's three faces are all split (6). With 4 end faces the total is 4 + 2 + 6 + 4 = 16.

questions.text: In 2018, a person spent half the time working, a third in sleeping and one-eighth in cooking. He spent the rest of the time exercising. How many total hours did he spend exercising?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The fraction left for exercise is \(1 - \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{24}\). 2018 is not a leap year, so it has 365 x 24 hours. One twenty-fourth of that is 365 hours.

questions.text: If the given shape in the figure is used to tile the grid on the right without any overlaps, what is the minimum number of units that will be left uncovered? Flips and rotations are allowed.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The shape is an S (Z) tetromino of 4 units and the grid is 6 x 6 = 36 units. S tetrominoes cannot fill a rectangle completely, and trying all placements shows at most 8 pieces fit without overlap. 8 x 4 = 32 units are covered, leaving 36 minus 32 = 4 units uncovered.

questions.text: A rectangular wooden plank has another smaller rectangular hole cut into it as shown in the figure given below. What is the minimum number of cutting planes that can divide the wooden plank into four parts of equal volume?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: A plane parallel to the top face, halfway through the thickness, splits the plank into two equal slabs, each a rectangle with a rectangular hole. A vertical plane through the centre of the plank and the centre of the hole halves any such shape, so it halves both slabs at once. Two intersecting planes give four parts of equal volume, and one plane can only give two parts.

questions.text: Count the number of differences between the two images shown below.
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Compare the two pictures region by region: face, shirt, the glass and straw on the left, the bowls on the table, the cups and spoons in front and the small items near the plate on the right. Seven spots differ between them.

questions.text: An intersection is where two or more lines and/or curves meet or cross. How many intersections are there in the figure?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: The figure has a large circle, a small circle above and one below, four small circles in a row across the middle, and a fifth curve in the centre that is an open arc ending on the bottom circle. Count the crossing points for each pair of curves (two per overlapping pair of circles), only on the drawn part of the arc, and add the two points where the arc ends on the bottom circle. This gives 44 points; no three curves pass through the same point.

questions.text: There are different types of pineapples in the given figure. How many pineapples appear only once?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Sort the pineapples by body pattern: black with white crescents, black with white L marks, black with white V marks, white with crescents, white with L marks, white with V marks, thin wavy lines, thick black wavy stripes, white lattice, black lattice and black with white dots. Every type repeats except the black pineapple with white dots and the black pineapple with a black lattice (white lines). So 2 pineapples appear only once.

questions.text: Two transparent discs with markings on them are shown. Which of the options can be created by overlapping and/or rotating them?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Each disc turns as a whole, so its marks keep their places relative to its own cross. On the red disc the dot sits just above the left arm and the triangle just below the right arm; on the black disc the square and hexagon keep fixed angles to the tilted black cross. C is the two discs laid together unturned. In A the red disc is turned 45 degrees (red cross becomes an X, dot and triangle move with it and the triangle tilts) and the black disc is turned until its cross is upright, carrying the square and hexagon with it. In B the dot and triangle are no longer on opposite sides of the red cross, and in D the red cross is turned but the dot has not moved, so B and D are impossible.

questions.text:
… Turkle describes the computer as an evocative object, one that raises new questions regarding our common sense of the distinction between artefacts and intelligent others. Her studies include an examination of the impact of computer-based artefacts on children’s conceptions of the difference between categories such as “alive” versus “not alive” and “machine” versus “person.” In dealing with the questions that computer-based objects evoke, children make clear that the differentiation of physical from psychological entities, which as adults we largely take for granted, is the end product of a process of establishing the relationship between the observable behaviour of a thing and its underlying nature. Children have a tendency, for example, to attribute life to physical objects on the basis of behaviours such as autonomous motion or reactivity, though they reserve humanity for entities evidencing such things as emotion, speech, and apparent thought or purposefulness. Turkle’s observation with respect to computational artefacts is that children ascribe to them an “almost aliveness” and a psychology, while maintaining their distinctness from human beings: a view that, as Turkle points out, is remarkable among other things for its correspondence to the views held by those who are the artefacts’ designers.

Read the paragraph given below and answer the question that follows:
Which of the following statements is/are TRUE of the paragraph above?

options.label: A
options.text: Turkle argues that children get confused when encountering computational artefacts and mistake them as human-like

options.label: B
options.text: Turkle argues that children are able to differentiate between physical and psychological entities by establishing relationship between how a thing behaves and its nature

options.label: C
options.text: Turkle concludes that children and adults react and categorise computer-based artefacts in a similar manner

options.label: D
options.text: Turkle finally concludes that children have a hard time understanding computer artefacts whereas adults can understand these artefacts far more easily.

questions.subject: Language
questions.solution: The paragraph says children separate physical from psychological entities by linking how a thing behaves to its underlying nature, which is statement B. A is wrong: children keep computers distinct from human beings, giving them only an almost aliveness. C is wrong: the passage only says the children's view matches the view of the artefacts' designers, not of adults in general. D is never stated.

questions.text: Shown below is a T-shaped image on a transparent sheet of paper. Which of the options IS/ARE made by overlapping and/or rotating multiple copies of the transparent sheet?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Every line in an option must be part of the outline of some T, and every T placed must have its whole outline present, because the sheets are transparent and no line can disappear. A, C and D can each be built from five T outlines that together give exactly the lines shown. In B the bottom row of five squares forces a T whose bar covers the three left squares, which would draw a line across the middle column at the bottom; that line is missing, so B cannot be made.

questions.text:
Five friends Puru, Qadir, Roy, Sham and Tom live on five vertices of a regular pentagonal ground in a clockwise order. One day while Puru was walking to meet Roy, met Qadir who was on the way to meet Tom. Qadir changed his mind and decided to go with Puru to meet Roy. After meeting Roy all three went to Tom’s house for a cup of tea.

If all of them took shortest routes cutting through the ground, which of the following statements is/are TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Till Tom’s place, Qadir walked more distance than Puru

options.label: B
options.text: Till Tom’s place, Puru walked more distance than Qadir

options.label: C
options.text: Till Tom’s place, Qadir walked double the distance than Roy

options.label: D
options.text: While returning to their respective homes from Tom’s place, Puru has to travel the least.

questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Take the side as 1; a diagonal is about 1.618. Puru walks along diagonal PR and Qadir along diagonal QT; these cross 0.618 from P and 0.618 from Q. Then both walk the remaining 1 to Roy and the diagonal RT (1.618) to Tom, so each walks 3.236 and A and B are false. Roy walks only RT = 1.618, exactly half of Qadir's distance, so C is true. Going home from Tom's, Puru walks one side (1) while Qadir and Roy each walk a diagonal (1.618), so D is true.

questions.text: A sphere, a cylinder and a cone, with equal heights are resting on a surface along a straight line. If the source of light is fixed and the light rays are parallel, which of the options show(s) the shadows correctly?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: With parallel rays all shadows point the same way, and their lengths depend on shape. The cylinder's flat top at full height throws the longest shadow, a long rounded strip. The sphere's shadow is an ellipse that reaches past the cone's tip, and the cone throws a pointed triangle. A and C show the cylinder's shadow longest, then the sphere, then the cone. In B and D the cylinder's shadow is about as short as the sphere's, which is impossible.

questions.text: Which of the following statements would you consider to be TRUE about the hour and minute hands of analogue clocks?

options.label: A
options.text: The hour hand and the minute hand would make 90 degrees angle with each other 24 times in a day

options.label: B
options.text: The hour hand and minute hand will overlap less than 24 times in a day

options.label: C
options.text: The hour hand and minute hand will overlap exactly on the hour number marker only once every half a day

options.label: D
options.text: The hour hand and minute hand will make acute angle to each other for almost as long as it will make obtuse angle to each other during the entire day

questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The hands are at right angles 44 times a day, not 24, so A is false. They overlap 22 times a day, fewer than 24, so B is true. In 12 hours they overlap 11 times, at positions 360/11 degrees apart, and only the overlap at 12 o'clock falls on an hour marker, so C is true. The angle between the hands grows at a steady rate and sweeps 0 to 180 degrees evenly, so the hands spend about as long at an acute angle as at an obtuse one, and D is true.

questions.text: Two friendly bugs were on their usual walk in the north-east direction. When the sun was in the east, they had an argument and one of them turned 45 degrees anticlockwise and walked away. Which of the images below correctly represent(s) their shadow now, when viewed by a person from top?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: After the turn one bug faces north and the other still faces north-east, so the north-facing bug points 45 degrees anticlockwise of the other; this fixes which way is north in each picture. With the sun in the east, both shadows fall to the west, which is to the left of the north-facing bug, and that bug should be the one that moved off to the west side. In B north is up-left, so west is down-left, and both shadows fall down-left. In D north points down the page, so west is to the right, and both shadows fall right. In A both shadows fall to the east, and in C the shadows point the wrong way for the bugs' headings.

questions.text: A pencil with pentagonal cross-section was sharpened using a pencil sharpener. Which of the options correctly represent(s) side view of the pencil?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: The sharpener cuts a cone. Each flat face is nearest the pencil's axis at its middle and farthest at its edges, so the cone cuts deepest into the middle of each face: the paint on each face ends in a curve that dips down in the middle and rises at the face's edges. B (two faces seen from an edge, one wider) and D (one face seen straight on with two thin side faces) show this. A shows the painted edge rising in the middle of each face, and C mixes the two, so both are wrong.

questions.text: A paper strip with a different colour on each side is joined as shown in the figure. If this strip is cut along the dashed line, which of the options correctly represent(s) the result(s)?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning

questions.text: Sundays are longer than Mondays. Mondays are shorter than Fridays. Wednesdays are shorter than Saturdays, which are in turn shorter than Sundays. Thursdays are shorter than Saturdays. Tuesdays are longer than Saturdays. Wednesdays and Thursdays are both longer than Fridays. If all of these are true, which of the options is/are also TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: Wednesdays could be as long as Thursdays.

options.label: B
options.text: Tuesdays could be the longest days of the week.

options.label: C
options.text: Mondays are the shortest days of the week.

options.label: D
options.text: Fridays could be as long as Sundays.

questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The chain is Monday < Friday < (Wednesday, Thursday) < Saturday < (Sunday, Tuesday). Wednesday and Thursday are never compared, so they could be equal (A). Tuesday and Sunday are never compared, so Tuesday could be longest (B). Every other day is longer than Friday or Sunday, which are longer than Monday, so Monday is the shortest (C). Friday is shorter than Wednesday, which is shorter than Saturday and Sunday, so D is false.

questions.text: Which of the options CANNOT be folded along the dotted lines into a package as shown in the image? For simplicity sake, cut lines have not been shown in the given schematic. The cross section of the package is an equilateral triangle.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The package is a triangular tube, so a net needs three equal panels between fold lines plus a narrow flap whose tabs push into the white slits on the far panel. A, B and C each have three equal panels, a flap of the right depth and tabs lined up with the slits. In D the top panel runs from the top edge to the first fold with no fold line where the overlap should start, so it is longer than the other two and cannot close into an equilateral triangle.

questions.text: Each of the options shows a pair of two different pieces. Which of the options CAN NOT be cut out of the given figure?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.subtopic: Matching a part to the whole
questions.solution: Match each diamond piece to a spot on the figure. A: the head and shoulder line, and the left arm slit with the top of the gap between the legs; both fit. C: the end of the left arm, and the two legs with their gap; both fit. In B the first piece fits the left shoulder, but in the second piece the slit begins level with the middle while the space beside it is plain white to the top corner; at the left arm the rounded shoulder would show in that corner, so it cannot be cut. In D the first piece fits the right shoulder and arm, but the second piece puts the bottom of the arm almost level with the top of the leg gap, while on the figure the arm ends well below that point.

questions.text: Shown below is an image that represents how cups should stack on top of each other in a stable manner. Among the given different types of cups, which of the cups CANNOT stack on itself in a stable manner?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge

questions.text: In the image shown, objects have been duplicated and rotated. Which object(s) is/are NOT arranged around a perfect circle?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Fit a circle through the centres of each kind of object. The pairs of ellipses (A) and the teal dot with orange crescent (B) all sit on circles to within a fraction of a pixel. The pink blobs (C) are off their best circle by up to about 13 pixels and the green squares (D) by up to about 40 pixels, so those two sets are not on perfect circles.

questions.text: Figures 2 and 3 can be derived from figure 1 by overlapping some of the given options one at a time. If flipping and rotations are allowed, which option(s) will allow you to derive figure 2 and 3?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Options A, B and C are the same piece: B is A flipped top to bottom and C is A flipped left to right (fork, single stub and zig-zag arm sit on matching vertices). D differs: one fork is replaced by a bent stub and an extra stub is added. Since flips are allowed, A, B and C stand or fall together; the A-type piece, laid over the hexagons, adds the Y-shaped lines that turn each hexagon into a cube in figures 2 and 3.

questions.text: P, Q, R, S, T, U and V are bees living in separate cells of a 2D hive made of hexagonal cells. T and V are neighbours of P. R and S are neighbours of U. V does not share a wall with T, U or R. Q, being the queen, shares a wall with everyone. Which of the options must be TRUE?

options.label: C
options.text: P and U share a wall

options.label: D
options.text: S and T are not neighbours

questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Q touches all six others, so they form a ring around Q, and in that ring each cell touches only its two ring neighbours. P lies between T and V, and U lies between R and S. V's other ring neighbour cannot be T, U or R, so it is S; then U follows S and R follows U, closing the ring T, P, V, S, U, R. So S and V are neighbours (A), R and T are neighbours (B), P and U are not (C false), and S touches only V, U and Q, so S and T are not neighbours (D).

questions.text: The figures show four different schematics of two flexible strings. If all the ends are pulled tight, which of the options will form a knot?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge

questions.text: Seven identical playing dice are unfolded in an identical manner. Six of the unfolded dice are laid out on a flat surface and are arranged to touch each other without overlapping. The figure shows a portion of the arrangement. Which face(s) from the seventh unfolded dice CAN NOT replace X if overlap must be avoided?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The complete green net shows the layout: a strip 2, 4, 5, 3 with 6 above the 4 and 1 below it. X is boxed in on the left, top and right, so the face placed there must be the only face on its edge of the net, with the rest of the net going downward. That is possible for 6, 1, 2 and 3 (an end face), but never for 4 or 5, which have net neighbours on two opposite sides. Turning the net so that 2 sits on top makes its two dots vertical, as in D, and turning it so that 3 sits on top makes its triangle point left, as in B. So 4 (A) and 5 (C) cannot replace X.

questions.text: Which option will replace the question mark?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Each figure has three rings of dots: 8 purple on the outside, 7 green in the middle and 5 orange inside, and each ring turns by its own fixed step from one figure to the next. The purple ring turns by two of its twelve places each time and the green ring turns back by one place each time, while the orange ring turns a little (about 15 degrees) each time. Continuing all three rings one more step gives the arrangement in option A. Options B and C repeat the fourth figure's purple ring, and options B and D have the wrong orange ring.

questions.text: A paper strip is rolled and then cut with two planes at 45 degree as shown below. The middle part of the cut paper is unrolled. Which of the options represents this part?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: A plane cutting a rolled strip at a slant crosses every turn of the roll, so when the strip is unrolled each cut edge becomes a wave: one rise and fall for each turn. The inner turns are shorter than the outer ones, so the waves change length along the strip. Match the two cut edges of the middle part, turn by turn, against the options. The unrolled middle part is C.

questions.text: The phrase shown below uses a particular font. Which of the options belongs to the same font?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: The phrase is set in an upright, loopless Thai font with square stroke ends and a raised, slanted flag at the top right of letters such as the ra and cho chang. Option A is slanted, option C has rounded stroke ends, and option B has a flat top with no flag. Option D is upright, square-ended and carries the same slanted top flag, so it matches.

questions.text: Aastha is sailing a paper boat in still water. Which of the given options represents the reflection correctly?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: A reflection in still water shows the scene as it would look from a point below the water surface, not simply the picture turned upside down. Aastha bends forward and looks down at the boat, so from below we should see more of her face and chin and less of the top of her head, with her eyes looking up towards the boat at the waterline. Options A and C just flip the top of her head into view, and in D her eyes look away from the boat. Option B shows the face from below with the eyes turned towards the boat.

questions.text: An illustration of a walking ant and a pair of glasses lying on the table surface is shown. Which is the correct illustration from the ant's current point of view?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Put yourself in the ant's place on the table: low down, at its position and facing the way it walks. Things near the ant look large and things farther away look small, and the arms and lenses of the glasses overlap in the order they stand from the ant. The illustration that shows the glasses from this low viewpoint, with the nearer parts larger and in front, is A.

questions.text:
If

drassoglitive means woodboard

frassopoolts means bodystudy

glitivedrassy means foodwood

dressowoolts means digitalscreen

Then which word would mean screensize
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: glitive appears in woodboard and foodwood, so glitive means wood, and the code words come in the reverse order of the English words. Then drasso means board, drassy means food, frasso means study, poolts means body, dresso means screen and woolts means digital. screensize in reverse order is size then screen, so the code must end in dresso and begin with a new word for size. drasso already means board, so issicsdresso is the answer.

questions.text: A rolled yellow paper cylinder is rotating clockwise direction at a constant rate of 1 revolution / 60 seconds. A pencil is touching the paper cylinder and is moving from T1 to T2 in 10 seconds and stops for 10 seconds. Then it moves to T3 in next 40 seconds (total time=60 seconds) as shown in figure 2. What would be the graph on paper when it is unrolled?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: One full turn takes 60 seconds, so the paper's width stands for 60 seconds and each 10 seconds is one sixth of it. The pencil rises the same height from T1 to T2 in 10 seconds (a steep straight line over one sixth), stays still for 10 seconds (a flat line over one sixth) and rises the same height again in 40 seconds (a gentle straight line over four sixths). Moving at steady speeds gives straight lines, not curves, so the trace is the one in option A, read from the red dot.

questions.text: An opaque circular disc is parallel to the table top. A beam of sunlight casts its shadow on the table top as shown in the figure. Which of the options represents the shape of the shadow as seen in the top view of the table?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Sunlight arrives as parallel rays. When a flat shape is parallel to the surface it is cast on, parallel rays shift the shape across without stretching it, whatever the angle of the light. So the disc's shadow on the table is a circle of the same size, seen from the top as option C. The ellipses in A, B and D would need the disc to be tilted relative to the table.

questions.text: In a given version of chess, no piece can capture another piece. Instead, each piece is on a mission. In the scenario shown in the figure on the left, the knight is on a mission to the diagonally opposite square marked by X. Assuming that no other piece moves, what is the minimum number of moves it will take the knight to reach there? (Note: In chess, the knight moves as shown in the figure on the right. The knight cannot land on any square that has a pawn, but can jump over it.)
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The knight starts at the bottom left corner (a1) and must reach the top right corner (h8). The pawns sit on f8, d7, e7, f7, b6, d5, f5, d4, h4, e3, f3, b2, g2 and f1. Even on an empty board a knight needs at least 6 moves to go from one corner to the opposite corner, so fewer than 6 is impossible. A 6-move route that avoids every pawn square exists: a1, b3, c5, e6, f4, g6, h8. So the minimum is 6.

questions.text: Three options are made out of the same set of pieces WITHOUT flipping. Which of the options is NOT possible?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Every figure uses the seven tangram pieces: two large triangles, one medium triangle, two small triangles, a square and a parallelogram. Triangles and the square look the same when flipped, but the parallelogram does not, so it decides the answer. In A, B and C the parallelogram leans the same way once turned. In D it is the mirror image of the others, which can only be made by flipping the piece, so D is not possible.

questions.text: A 10 cm tall card with some cut-outs is placed on a long table in front of a lamp in a dark room as shown in the figure. The lamp is 15 cm tall and is placed 15 cm in front of the card. Which of the options shows the correct shadow cast by the card?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: A point at height h on the card throws its shadow at a distance \(\frac{225}{15-h}\) cm from the lamp, so the card's foot lands at 15 cm and its top at 45 cm, and the shadow widens three times along its length. The higher a cut-out is, the more its shadow is stretched along the table: the circle near the bottom stays almost round, the star in the middle is stretched about one and a half times, and the triangle near the top is stretched about twice as long as it is wide. Option C shows a nearly round circle, a stretched star and a long triangle. A shortens the triangle and stretches the circle too much, B leaves the star unstretched, and D flattens the circle sideways.

questions.text: Which is the odd one out?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Each figure has a circle, a rectangle, a triangle, a rounded bar and five dots. In A, C and D one dot sits inside all four shapes and each of the other four dots sits inside exactly one shape, one dot for each shape. In B one dot lies inside both the circle and the rectangle, and no dot lies inside the circle alone. So B breaks the rule.

questions.text: Identify the correct set of legs for Mr. Kumar to balance his body as he carries a heavy box.
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Carrying a heavy box in front of him shifts Mr. Kumar's combined centre of gravity forwards, so to stay balanced it must stay above the area between his feet. He leans back from the hips and plants his legs so that his feet sit under the combined weight of his body and the box. The set of legs that does this is C.

questions.text: Front and back views of a solid are shown. Which of the options can be folded to form this solid?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The solid has a yellow square on top and a grey square at the bottom, each ringed by four sloping trapezoids, with a band of four rectangles between them. The two views show that two neighbouring sides are pink on the top slope and band and green on the bottom slope, while the other two sides are green on the top slope and band and pink on the bottom slope. Net A has only three band rectangles and net D gives one side two band rectangles and another none. In net C one side folds up with a green top slope over a pink band. Net B folds into four sides that match the views exactly.

questions.text: Shown below is a paint splatter on a wall surface. A paint squeegee is pulled over it. Which of the options correctly represents the part of the pattern formed?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: The squeegee drags each blob of paint straight down, so every vertical line through the splatter that touches paint becomes a stripe, as wide as the paint is across at that line. Reading the splatter from left to right gives two thin stripes, the wide central band, then five narrower stripes at fixed gaps. Option D has stripes in exactly those places and widths. A adds an extra stripe beside the band, B moves two of the right-hand stripes, and C makes the central band too narrow.

questions.text: The adjacent figure has six compartments. Each compartment consists of six squares. These squares are to be filled with six different colours in such a way that each row, each column and each compartment should have all six colours. Which of the options will replace the question marks?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The grid is a 6 by 6 puzzle with compartments 3 squares wide and 2 tall. In the middle-right compartment, row 3 already has yellow so its empty square is purple, and then column 6 forces green and yellow into row 4. Working on, row 1 must end in orange, the bottom-right compartment gives red and blue in row 5, and column 5 is left with green and blue for rows 1 and 2. Row 1 already has blue, so the top question mark (row 1, column 5) is green, and column 4 then leaves red for the other question mark (row 2, column 4). That is option C.

questions.text: A giant creature is walking towards a group of buildings in the city. Which is the correct perspective from the creature's point-of-view?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The creature stands to the left of the buildings with its eyes above most rooftops, so it looks down on them: nearer buildings sit lower in its view and farther ones higher, closer to the horizon. Only the tall white tower reaches about eye level, so its roof touches the horizon line. The short light-blue block is the nearest building, so it should be lowest, just below the far blue tower, and the grey and beige roofs, at about the same distance, should appear at about the same height. Option C keeps all of these relations; D puts the grey block too low and makes the light-blue block too large, A leaves a gap below the blue tower, and B drops the beige block too low.

questions.text: Which of the options will replace the question mark?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: Each frame shows the same shape of 11 hexagons: a group of 6, one linking hexagon and a group of 4. The whole shape turns 45 degrees anticlockwise from one frame to the next, so the fifth frame is the first one turned through 180 degrees, with the group of 4 on top and the group of 6 below. At the same time the pink dot steps to a neighbouring cell inside the group of 6 and the green dot steps around the group of 4, reaching the linking cell in the fifth frame. Option B shows the shape turned 180 degrees with the dots in those cells; A is turned 270 degrees, and C and D are turned 225 degrees.

questions.text: The figure shows a mechanism with a disc, two bars and a static surface connected to each other with hinges. The disc rotates about the hinge at its centre as shown. What is the path traced by point X (end point of the longest bar) in this planar set up?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: This is a four-bar linkage: the pin on the disc goes round a circle, the short upright bar can only swing about its hinge on the ground, and the long bar joins the two and carries X beyond the upright bar's top. As the disc turns, the end of the long bar near the disc swings round a full circle while the upper hinge only rocks back and forth. So X traces a closed loop that is rounded at the end near the disc and tapers to a narrow tip on the far side, with an arched upper edge. Plotting the positions of X for a full turn of the disc gives the shape in option D.

questions.text: Identify the correct representation of lighting for this scene, given that the lightening strike is the only light source.
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: The lightning strikes behind the front row of buildings, so the faces of those buildings that we see point away from the light and must be dark, with the sky and buildings around the bolt glowing. That rules out B and C, where the front buildings are brightly lit. Between A and D, the light should fall most strongly on the clouds and background walls that face the bolt; in A the clouds glow around the bolt and the background buildings are lit on the sides facing it, while in D they are lit on the sides facing away.

questions.text: Which of the following lakes has the largest area?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The lakes are made of straight-sided blocks, so their areas can be compared by fitting them onto a common grid or by comparing the blocks they are built from. A, B and C come out close to one another, but D is wider through its middle and long, and covers more than 10 percent more area than any of the others. So D is the largest lake.

questions.text: Which of the given options matches the patterns (1,2,3,4) with tiles (P,Q,R,S) correctly?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Turn each pattern until its bricks lie level and upright, then look for the four-brick group of each tile. Pattern 1 contains the two orange-then-purple L shapes of R, and pattern 3 contains the diagonal run of two flat bricks followed by two upright ones in P. Pattern 2 contains S, an orange flat-and-upright pair followed by a purple upright-and-flat pair. That leaves Q for pattern 4, which is option D.

questions.text: Which of the options correctly shows the silhouettes of the given image?
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: A silhouette is the filled outline of the picture, so it must keep every part of the outline: each raised hand, the gaps between heads and between legs, and the hands holding the flag pole. Compare each option with the picture region by region and reject it at the first place where the outline is filled in or cut away differently. Only B matches the picture everywhere.

questions.text: Three rings are shown in the figure. They roll in the specified directions and stop when centres of all the rings coincide at line XX'. What pattern would they make?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: A ring rolling without slipping turns by the distance rolled divided by its radius. The left ring rolls about a quarter of its circumference to the right, so it turns about 90 degrees clockwise and its curved band moves from the bottom to the left side. The middle ring rolls about the same distance to the left, turning about 90 degrees anticlockwise, so its band moves from the bottom to the right side. The right ring rolls about twice as far, turning about 180 degrees, so its straight bar now runs from the left down to the lower right. Overlaying the three gives option B.

questions.text: Figure shows a clothes line attached to four independent pulleys P, Q, R & S. Which of the options represent the correct rotation of pulleys that would result in lowering the clothes line?
questions.subject: Practical and Scientific Knowledge
questions.solution: Lowering the line means the hangers move down, so each rope moves along its path from the hand towards the hangers. Follow each rope round its pulley. The rope to Q runs over Q's top and across to R's top, then down R's right side to the hand: as the line lowers, it moves left across the tops of both, so Q and R turn anticlockwise. The other rope rises from the hanger under P's right side and runs along to S, then over S and down to the hand: P's right side moves down, so P turns clockwise, while S's top moves left, so S turns anticlockwise. That is C.

questions.text: Which of the options will replace the question mark?
questions.subject: Analytical and Logical Reasoning
questions.solution: The squares walk around the twelve-colour artist's colour wheel: green, blue-green, blue, blue-violet, violet, red-violet, red, red-orange. The next colour after red-orange on that wheel is orange, which is option A. Yellow-orange (B), yellow (C) and yellow-green (D) come after it.

questions.text:
Assume that the English alphabet was redesigned, and the new alphabet had alternating upper case and lower case letters. The alphabet starts with uppercase A, and

1) all upper case letters were rotated clockwise by 90 degrees
2) all lower case letters were rotated anti-clock wise by 90 degrees

Using the new alphabet, the word "HELP" would be written as:
questions.subject: Observation and Design Sensitivity
questions.solution: Letters in odd positions are upper case and letters in even positions are lower case, so H (8th) is h, E (5th) is E, L (12th) is l and P (16th) is p. Turning h anticlockwise lays its stem flat along the bottom with the arch on the right, E turned clockwise lays its spine along the top with three prongs pointing down, the handwritten l turned anticlockwise puts its loop on the left, and p turned anticlockwise lays its stem flat with the bowl on top of the left half. Option A shows exactly these four shapes. C turns the E the wrong way, B uses the wrong letters, and D turns the l and p the wrong way.

questions.text: If the given figure represents a cube in 3D, which of the options correctly represents its views from different sides?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The drawing is a cube with hatching on its faces, and each option shows its views from different sides. The hatch lines on each view must run the way the face's lines run in the drawing. Options C and D differ only in how closely the lines are drawn on one view, so more than one option can be argued correct, and IIT Bombay gave every candidate full marks.

questions.text: A square is cut into 4 pieces. One of the pieces is shown on the left and the remaining three are in the options. Which of the options is NOT a part of the square?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Count the unit squares: the given piece has 4, A has 4, B has 3, C has 4 and D has 5, 20 in all. A 4 by 4 square holds 16, so the piece that is not part of the square must have exactly 4 squares, and both A and C do. Since more than one answer can be justified, IIT Bombay gave every candidate full marks.

questions.text: In the figure given below which of the options will replace the question mark?
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: Every cell is drawn from parts of an outer hexagon and an inner pentagon with lines to its centre. In each row, the third cell keeps every hexagon side that appears in either of the first two cells, but only the inner lines that appear in both of them. In the last row the two cells together cover all six hexagon sides, and the only inner lines they share are the left and upward lines from the centre. So the missing cell is a complete hexagon with just those two inner lines, which is option B.

questions.text: Which of the options can be associated with all the objects?
questions.subject: Creativity
questions.solution: The objects are a film strip, a light bulb, a ship, a man shooting, a compass rose marked N and a fish. Each pairs with the word star: film star, a star as a source of light, starship, shooting star, the North (pole) star and starfish. A square, circle or triangle does not link to all six, so the star in option C is the answer.

questions.text: Select the correct option.
questions.subject: Visualization and Spatial Reasoning
questions.solution: The sheet is folded right half over left, then top half down, then right half over left again, giving a piece one quarter as wide and half as tall, and a slanted hole is cut through all eight layers. Unfolding reflects the hole across each fold line in turn, giving four holes along the top and four along the bottom, mirrored about the centre line and about the middle fold. Along the bottom, the centre pair lean towards each other at the bottom and meet there in a V, and along the top they meet at the top, with the end holes leaning to match. Option A shows this arrangement; B and D have the end holes leaning the wrong way, and C has the top centre pair meeting at the bottom.
